title: Incident response: evidence retention, escalation roles, and SIEM mapping guide
content:
Purpose and scope:
This working guide defines practical steps for retaining and preserving evidence during security incidents, clarifies escalation and human-review responsibilities under RBAC v2, and provides pragmatic SIEM field-mapping and export/query examples to support rapid triage and post-incident analysis. It is meant for on-call responders, SREs assisting investigations, security engineers automating evidence capture, and product/privacy leads when user data is implicated.

Key principles (summary):
- Preserve first: assume any relevant logs, artifacts, or host snapshots will be needed for later forensic analysis.
- Least privilege during collection: use RBAC v2 temporary elevation tokens where possible and log every elevation.
- Chain of custody: record who accessed what and when; prefer automated, signed artifacts.
- Keep exports reproducible: include query text, time ranges, and export hashes.
- Retention parity: ensure evidence retention policy aligns with legal/compliance and SIEM retention windows.

Escalation matrix and roles (RBAC v2 alignment):
- Level 0 (Alert triage): Security on-call engineer (role: sec_oncall). Responsibilities: initial triage, artifact snapshot (short-term), open incident ticket, attach initial SIEM query results.
- Level 1 (Investigation lead): Incident investigator (role: sec_investigator). Responsibilities: coordinate evidence preservation, request host snapshots from SRE, request additional logs from service owners, update incident severity and SLAs.
- Level 2 (Containment and remediation): Product/SRE lead with write-capable role (role: sec_containment). Uses temporary elevation tokens (duration <= 2 hours) granted via RBAC v2 admin flow. Must create a signed gazette entry describing actions and reason.
- Legal / Privacy / CS Notification: Legal counsel / privacy lead (role: privacy_review) and Customer Success (role: cs_notify) are notified per incident policy (severity threshold or exfiltration suspected).

RBAC v2 guidance for evidence-preserving actions:
- Use short-lived Just-In-Time (JIT) grants for any account that makes irreversible changes (e.g., user data deletion, config rollbacks). Log JIT grant id in the incident ticket.
- Create read-only service accounts for evidence collection (role: evidence_reader) and prefer them over human accounts for automated capture to reduce noise in chain-of-custody.
- Audit every elevation: record principal, scope, start/end time, and approval ticket id. Retain elevation logs for at least 1 year or per legal retention requirement.

Immediate preservation checklist (Level 0 -> Level 1 handoff):
1) Freeze time window: determine earliest suspected intrusion_time and freeze the end_time for initial capture (document both as UTC).
2) Preserve SIEM snapshot: run named queries (below), export raw event JSON, and compute SHA256 for each export file.
3) Host evidence: request ephemeral host snapshot (memory + disk delta) from SRE or use existing forensic appliance. Tag snapshot with incident id, requester, and TTL.
4) Application logs: pull structured logs for impacted services covering [earliestObserved - 2h, latestObserved + 1h]. Prefer raw log lines with sequence ids.
5) Auth events: collect audit logs focused on token issuance, RBAC grants, OAuth changes, API key lifecycle events, and admin console login attempts.
6) Config and deployment metadata: capture deployment manifests, image digests, config diffs, and autoscaler events for the time window.
7) Evidence index: add each artifact to a simple evidence index (CSV): incident_id, artifact_type, path_or_s3_uri, sha256, collector, timestamp_utc, retention_until.

Suggested SIEM field mapping (canonical fields to support exports and downstream tooling):
- canonical.timestamp -> event.time (ISO8601 UTC)
- canonical.source -> event.source (kubernetes/pod, host, auth, api)
- canonical.user_id -> identity.user.id
- canonical.user_email -> identity.user.email
- canonical.principal -> identity.principal (service_account|human)
- canonical.action -> event.action (login, token_issue, exec, file_read, config_change)
- canonical.result -> event.outcome (success|failure|unknown)
- canonical.ip -> network.client.ip
- canonical.request_id -> trace.request_id
- canonical.raw_payload -> event.raw (base64 or escaped JSON)

Maintaining consistency: when exporting from any audit store (GCS logs, k8s audit, app logs, auth logs), transform to the canonical schema above before storing in the long-term evidence bucket. Include original raw event in addition to the normalized row.

SIEM export and query examples (Ops-friendly snippets):
- Splunk/ELK style pseudo-query to fetch suspicious admin token issuance:
  index=auth_logs source=oauth_server event.action="token_issue" event.outcome="success" | where identity.user.email!="service@redwood.com" | stats count by identity.user.email, network.client.ip

- Kibana/ES DSL (example) to locate RBAC elevation events:
  {"query":{"bool":{"must":[{"term":{"event.action":"rbac_grant"}},{"range":{"event.time":{"gte":"2026-02-10T00:00:00Z","lte":"2026-02-10T04:00:00Z"}}}]}}}

- Prioritized quick-queries (to run immediately):
  1) Admin console auth failures in last 1h: event.source:auth_console AND event.outcome:failure | top identity.user.email
  2) New service-account creation in last 24h: event.action:service_account_create | table event.time, identity.principal, trace.request_id
  3) Large outbound data transfer: network.bytes_out > 100000000 | stats sum(network.bytes_out) by host

Formatting exports for forensic consumption:
- For each export: include a manifest.json (flat file) with fields: incident_id, collector, time_range_start, time_range_end, sha256, original_query, canonical_fields_present (comma separated).
- Store exports in: s3://redwood-incident-evidence/{incident_id}/{artifact_type}/{export-file}. Keep access restricted to incident principals.

Automated evidence capture patterns (recommended):
- SIEM-triggered export webhooks: when an alert matches severity >= P2, push raw event batch to the incident bucket and create a signed manifest.
- On-call bot integration: on incident creation, bot runs baseline queries (auth failures, RBAC grants, suspicious execs) and attaches artifacts to the ticket.
- Immutable snapshots: when possible, mount forensic snapshots as read-only and create checksums of files that investigators will reference rather than handing out copies.

Human review checklist (for investigators):
- Confirm identity and scope: verify which principals, services, and time windows are implicated.
- Validate provenance: ensure each artifact has a checksum and matching manifest entry.
- Correlate events: link request_id across app logs, tracing, and network logs.
- Look for privilege creep: sequence of actions that escalate capability (create service account -> add role -> issue token).
- Avoid altering evidence: if live investigation requires executing commands on host, run them from an evidence_reader account and capture the entire session.

Retention, deletion, and legal holds:
- Default evidence retention: 180 days for incident artifacts in the evidence bucket unless legal hold is applied.
- SIEM retention: adhere to SIEM hot/cold tier policies; copy canonical incident slices to the evidence bucket before the hot window expires.
- Legal hold flow: Legal can request 'hold' on an incident id — compliance lead toggles retention_until -> indefinite, notifies SRE to prevent lifecycle cleanup. Document hold id in incident ticket.

Post-incident: handoff and postmortem inputs:
- The investigator produces an evidence index and a short forensic summary (2–3 paragraphs) describing key artifacts and confidence levels.
- Attach canonical queries used for the investigation to the postmortem and store them under /postmortems/{incident_id}/queries.txt.
- Redaction notes: if user PII is included in evidence, produce a redacted export for cross-team consumption and keep unredacted artifacts restricted to legal/investigators.

Automation and SRE tasks backlog (ideas to reduce manual friction):
- Auto-populate evidence index entries when SIEM exports to evidence bucket.
- RBAC v2 audit enhancer: cross-reference JIT grants with incident tickets and flag mismatches.
- Pre-built snapshot playbooks per service to standardize what to collect (k8s: pod logs + container filesystem diff; DB: binlog slices + auth events).

Appendix: quick templates and example entries
- Evidence index CSV example row:
  INCIDENT-2026-0023,siem_export,s3://redwood-incident-evidence/INCIDENT-2026-0023/siem/export-2026-02-20-11z.json,9c7a2f...,,maya.patel@redwood.com,2026-02-20T11:23:05Z,2027-02-20T11:23:05Z

- Minimal manifest.json example (flat):
  { "incident_id": "INCIDENT-2026-0023", "collector": "sec-oncall-bot", "time_range_start": "2026-02-20T10:00:00Z", "time_range_end": "2026-02-20T11:00:00Z", "sha256": "9c7a2f...", "original_query": "index=auth_logs event.action=token_issue event.outcome=failure" }

Notes and open questions (working):
- We need to finalize a single canonical storage location and lifecycle policy for evidence (S3 vs GCS) and coordinate with backups and cost owners.
- Decision required: maximum JIT grant duration for remediation actions (proposal: 2 hours, extend only with two-person approval).
- Need a small set of pre-approved read-only evidence collectors per service to avoid ad-hoc human collection.

Contact and ownership:
- Doc owner: Maya Patel (security engineer)
- Primary on-call escalation: sec-oncall rotation (see internal schedule)
- Policy owner: Priya Kapoor (security compliance)

This document is a working draft intended to be refined after the next tabletop exercise. Please add comments, attach relevant ticket links, and flag any steps that break automated test coverage or infra constraints.
